text.p: Business travelers who wonder how airlines treat their very best customers might want to check out a new facility at Chicago's O'Hare Internatonal Airport.

A select few passengers paying top dollar for first or business class seats and arriving at O'Hare after long overnight flights are being offered the use of luxurious "shower suites" where the tile floors and towel racks are heated and a valet is standing by to press clothes, shine shoes and get breakfast.
Such facilities are nothing new at airline clubs and lounges at busy international airports, but their number and variety is expanding as the airline industry goes after upscale customers.

"It's a competive business," says United spokesman Joe Hopkins. "If we can offer a service no one else has or if we can do it better than the other guy then some of this upper end business will move toward us."

United has or will soon offer the shower suites at London's Heathrow and at Miami International. The carrier is also offering similar services through hotels near two dozen airports to give arriving top-scale travelers a place to regroup and refresh before taking on the business day.
None of this, of course, is for the day-tripping business traveller making the rounds from Denver to Dayton and back.

Use of United's shower suites is by invitation and restricted to full-fare first and business class travelers at the end of overnight flights of five hour's duration or longer. In the case of the O'Hare facility, which features only four of the suites, the service will be offered initially to select passengers on flights coming from Hawaii and Alaska.
United's shower suites at Miami and Heathrow are bigger -- 13 rooms at each -- because there is more traffic of the kind warranting the service at those locations.

"All travel is expanding," Hopkins said. "If you look at our traffic this year we're up something like 3 or 4 percent -- its all expanding, first, business and economy. People are willing to pay the additional fare for business and first class but they expect more value."

Also growing, he said, is the use of airline clubs like the one at O'Hare in which the shower facility is located. United operates two "Red Carpet Clubs" at O'Hare, an airport where the carrier handles from 70,000 to 100,000 passengers daily.

The larger of its two clubs at O'Hare can seat 540 people and it's not unusual to find every seat filled at busy times, Hopkins said. Club members also have desk spaces with telephone connections where they can work with laptop computers.

The cost of membership for such clubs and the services offered vary by airline, and by how often the customer flies. United charges $300 dollars for a new member who is not in the airline's "premier" frequent flier class.
A good rundown on what's avialble at all of the clubs (some for instance have cash bars while in others, drinks are on the house) can be found in the September issue of Frequent Flyer Magazine.
